narrative:
Your application was reviewed by a predictive model that assessed your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and the model estimated a 51% probability that you would not pass — a result that sits right on the edge of the decision boundary, meaning your situation is genuinely close to the threshold for approval. Because the model predicted you would fail, your application was unfortunately rejected. It's important to understand that this decision was not based on your gender or race, and that the model is working with a snapshot of your academic and personal circumstances to make this assessment.

To help explain what drove this outcome, it's useful to think about "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your profile that would have been enough to flip the prediction from "fail" to "pass." These counterfactual scenarios don't change who you are, but they highlight which specific factors, if different, would have led to an approval. Three such scenarios were generated for your case, and they tell a remarkably consistent story.

Across all three alternative scenarios, only one thing changed: your LSAT score. In every single scenario, no other factor was adjusted — not your law school grades, not your family income, not your undergraduate GPA, and not your enrollment status. This means the model identified your LSAT score as the single most decisive factor standing between your current outcome and an approval. The average change needed across these scenarios was an increase of just 2 points on the LSAT, bringing your score from 34 to 36.

This is a meaningful finding because it points to a very specific and achievable target. Students who passed the bar exam had an average LSAT score of approximately 37, and your current score of 34 places you noticeably below that benchmark. Closing even part of that gap — specifically reaching a score of 36 — appears to be sufficient, according to the model's analysis, to shift the prediction in your favor.

What makes this particularly worth noting is that several other aspects of your profile are actually quite strong. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is well above the average of 3.24 among students who passed, which is a genuine asset. The model did not suggest you need to change your GPA, your enrollment status, or your family income situation in any of the scenarios, which means these factors are not what's holding your application back. The challenge lies specifically in the combination of your LSAT score alongside your law school academic performance, where your first- and third-year decile rankings of 3 and 1 respectively are considerably below the averages of around 6 seen among students who passed.

The most actionable path forward based on this analysis is to retake the LSAT with the goal of reaching at least a score of 36. Given that you are currently studying part-time, it may also be worth considering whether there are ways to dedicate more focused preparation time to LSAT study, as the consistency of this single change across all three scenarios suggests it carries significant weight in the model's assessment. Your strong undergraduate academic record shows you have the capability to perform at a high level, and channeling that strength into targeted LSAT preparation could be the key step that moves your application from rejected to approved.
